question: A 56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for the evaluation of a 3-day history of left lower abdominal pain. During this period, the patient has also had a low-grade fever and has not had a bowel movement. He has a history of constipation. He underwent a cholecystectomy at the age of 53 years. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the last 30 years. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows left lower quadrant tenderness with no guarding or rebound. There is no edema of his lower extremities. CT of the abdomen with contrast shows segmental wall thickening of the descending colon with multiple diverticula, surrounding fat stranding, and a 5.5-cm, low-attenuating pelvic fluid collection. Intravenous fluids and bowel rest are started. Treatment with intravenous morphine, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Diverticulitis -> Left lower abdominal pain -> Low-grade fever -> Constipation history -> Cholecystectomy history -> Smoking history -> Elevated temperature, pulse, and blood pressure -> Abdominal tenderness -> CT findings of segmental wall thickening, diverticula, fat stranding, and pelvic fluid collection -> Intravenous fluids and bowel rest -> Intravenous morphine, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole -> Possible abscess formation -> Need for drainage -> CT-guided percutaneous abscess drainage -> 80%
enhanced_information: The patient presents with diverticulitis evidenced by left lower abdominal pain, low-grade fever, constipation history, cholecystectomy history, smoking, and CT findings. The current management includes intravenous fluids, bowel rest, and antibiotics. Given the possible abscess formation indicated by the CT, the most appropriate next step is CT-guided percutaneous abscess drainage to address the 5.5-cm pelvic fluid collection.
analysis: The patient presents with diverticulitis complicated by a pelvic fluid collection, indicating possible abscess formation. The current management includes antibiotics and supportive care. Given the size of the abscess and the need for intervention, the most appropriate next step is CT-guided percutaneous abscess drainage to address the 5.5-cm pelvic fluid collection.
